quotes.text: My earliest memory goes way back, I got my first drum set when I was just a 10-month-old baby. I took a few lessons from the drummers in my dad's bands at that age, and I used to play rock music with them. My father is a composer and would constantly play classical and jazz music in our small apartment, so I was always surrounded by his compositions and musical inspirations since birth. One of my strongest memories is crying when he played Bartók for me when I was around 3 or 4 years old and I had no idea why I was crying.

The artists who have really influenced my creative process include Kraftwerk, Iron Maiden, Joy Division, Nirvana, Gesaffelstein, SosMula, Magma, Stockhausen, Mozart, Bach, Coltrane, Miles Davis… What inspires me isn't just their music, but the distinct states of mind that come with it.

It feels almost like a divine mission. I have the sensation the music I make already exists in my mind before I create it. It comes through memories, images tied to certain smells that emerge when I play a few notes on the piano, like a mental archeology turn into the future by composition. It's like observing unknown places with a flashlight, places I illuminate and reveal through sound. Some of these mental landscapes have yet to be explored, given the vastness of what we don't yet know about our universe. Music is like a language to me, I learned it at the same time I was learning to speak. I can improvise endlessly the way we're having a conversation now. To me, nature and the world around us are the only true forms of artistic creation, and my music simply reflects my emotional responses to natural and psychic phenomena I experience volontary or not. These deeply personal and emotional events are what drive me to create.

It's very diverse, which is great for personal growth, especially the underground scene. But to be honest, my musical culture is deeply Anglo-Saxon. I don't really connect with most of the mainstream French music, except for a few rare exceptions for sure, i'm not closed to nothing but those artists usually have Anglo influences too ahah, France is a very rational, conservative, and literary country, it's not very Rock'n'Roll in France, to be honest. If you don't fit into the box, you're quickly seen as a degenerate ahah, in my opinion, France hasn't innovated musically in a long time.

My influences have certainly evolved in many ways over the years, but at the core of everything is my passion for UK garage and its influence on me has always been there. As a 15 year old getting into production, with 10 years of classical music training before that, I started making beats and writing music with such a big variety of influences. I'm always on the lookout for new producers, alongside watching lots of films and listening to their soundtracks. I just never stop soaking in the music around me to be honest. I feel it's important to stay up to date with new musical directions and production styles, while always holding on to my true artistic feelings and never forcing anything. If it feels right and hits me whilst I'm making it, I'm there for the ride and can't see that ever changing.

From an early stage, I was very much influenced by the dark side of UK garage around 2003 – 2005, artists like Wookie, Jaimeson, Sticky and Zinc, Youngstar etc. I also loved the more soulful and melodic side of garage, people like MJ Cole and Todd Edwards. Then, I discovered Burial and the world of more abstract, deep and moody garage/dubstep. Alongside that, I was really getting into dubstep and the early sounds from 2007 onwards. This collection of various styles and sounds all helped morph where my mind goes when making music. Fast forward to today, I'm still loving the garage scene and where it's evolved too, I'd say garage and breaks are in such a good place at the moment, whilst dubstep still excites me and drives my creativity too.

The only challenge I find is promoting the music after making it. On the creative side, I just dive into where my heads at, and also take influence from the new music I'm discovering at the time too. Navigating the industry is the challenge when you're an electronic artist that likes to make such a variety of moods and vibes. The rewards are being able to work alongside amazing artists like Lauren L'aimant and Leo Wood, and also being able to express myself fully, rather than staying in one lane that can end up becoming creatively stale or losing that excitement creativity provides.

With the #Mixtape series, it's all about a collection of tracks from different chapters and moments coming together as one project. Some of the tracks, like 'We Can Go' especially, have been in the locker for some time. Whereas the two vocal feature tracks were written with the Mixtape in mind. Ultimately I let my mind take me where I should be and having the project in focus gave me a good opportunity to explore that energy and mood. My mindset when making the more melodic and soulful tracks is so much different to when I'm making more bass heavy bangers. My vibey side is basically therapy, then I have to feed the beast in between with something harder.

There aren't any live instruments in this project actually, although I've used various instrument samples in the tracks – which I love to do. Most of the sounds though are from synths as I'm a sucker for retro sounding pads and keys. Arturia in particular and a great plugin called 'Spire' have been heavily used, alongside a wide variety of vocal and instrument samples that I've manipulated etc.

So with #Vibes, I worked with two vocalists, Lauren L'aimant and Leo Wood. The rest was written without any collaboration on this project, unlike the #Heaters mixtape – where every track was a collaboration. Working with both vocalists has been class too, both amazing singers and artists in their own right. As soon as I heard both acapellas, I was immersed in the creative side of both tracks until they were finished. They really got under my skin because the vocals are so strong.

I'd say Burial would be unreal, also Board of Canada. Love both of their styles and the way I get lost in their music. James Blake would be unreal too, love his music and voice. On a more bass heavy or grimey side, I'd love to work with D Double E,

I can clearly remember my first keyboard which allowed me to multi-track record on it, and save the projects/tracks to floppy disc, now that's a throwback right?! I was playing a piece called 'Fur Elise' by Mozart and recording it over a Yamaha stock UK Garage beat. No doubt with the volume full blast and slightly distorting.
Ah man, so many. Some of my inspirations over the years include Burial, Brian Eno, James Blake, Boards of Canada, Olafur Arnalds, Max Richter, Coki, Bicep, Alix Perez and Dillinja. Quite a spread!

Most of my inspiration comes from mood. The direction for a track mostly depends on what I'm doing in life, a show I've got coming up, a forthcoming release or just my general vibe on the day. I also get a lot of inspiration from films and soundtracks. Besides that, my vibey music is heavily inspired by my emotions, the way I feel when I see my kids playing and learning, my memories of growing up – whether good or bad – and my hopes for the future.

It can really vary depending on the project. For my deeper and darker, more bass heavy bangers that featured on my Mixtape 1: #Heaters, I'd say in front of a soundsystem, ideally a custom rig made by a crew – I've been super lucky to play on some sick systems over the years. For my more vibey sounds that are coming on Mixtape 2: #Vibes I'd say either on the move, watching the world go by, or on an adventure. I find myself listening to those sides of my music whilst travelling on tour a lot.

I always like to keep up to date with new artists and styles coming through the scenes, so I take a lot of inspiration and evolve as the time goes by too and to keep a fresh perspective. That said, I've always stayed true to what I love and my passions rather than following any trends – but my overall sound has definitely evolved on the technical side the longer I do this. I'm always striving to get the best sound possible, trying to replicate how it sounds in my head before I make it.
